seo.meta_title: Can You Say '수고하세요' to Your Boss? | Why AI Gets It Wrong
seo.meta_description: Translating '수고하세요' literally causes awkward workplace mistakes in Korea. Discover natural alternatives for superiors and elders.

ai_failure.situation: Saying goodbye to a boss or client at the end of the day
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Translates as a polite 'Keep up the good work' and recommends using it to anyone.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: Sounds condescending when used toward superiors or elders.

natural_solution.rule: Only use toward peers or subordinates. Never to superiors.

alternatives.context: Leaving the office before your boss/colleagues
Polite acknowledgment of shared hard work to senior colleagues

nuance: 수고하세요 literally asks the listener to keep enduring effort. Telling someone to keep working implies you are in a position to evaluate or direct their labor — which is the senior's role. That is why the phrase flows naturally downward or sideways (a customer to a cashier, a manager to a team) but feels presumptuous upward. Many Koreans also avoid it with elders entirely and switch to phrases that acknowledge effort already spent, like 고생 많으셨습니다.
